nodes.label: The old fat map
nodes.full: The folio opens on the two fat worlds that fats-300bc-600ad ends with: oil and ghee in the south and east, animal fat and butter in the north, with the church and the Islamic caliphate carrying the older oil culture across the break.

nodes.label: Monastic oil

nodes.label: Maya oil palms
nodes.full: Coyol, huiscoyol and cohune fill the fat gap left by lean deer and a short list of oily fruits; Copán cultivated coyol outright.

nodes.label: Pemba’s lone sesame seed
nodes.full: A single sesame seed at an early Swahili site may be a trace of the old Indian sesame-oil trade — or just a local wild plant.

edges: The church’s retention of oil expertise is the continuation across the break of the Mediterranean oil culture.
Soap making in Italy rests on olive oil in the Mediterranean, as Ward says, alongside the monastic oil that Mueller describes.
Both are dairy fats of the Atlantic fringe in the same centuries, one a luxury and one a stored surplus.
The Baghdad cookbook keeps the Near Eastern fat habit (tail fat, olive oil) that the Babylonian tablets show.
Both are Tang uses of fat in Buddhist practice, the lamp oil of the monastery and the ghee of the soul’s ladder.
Tang oil production and the monastery’s oil for its lamp belong to the same expansion of vegetable oil in China.
The Frankish estate rules and the Anglo-Saxon thane’s butter show the same northern fat economy from the stewards’ and the eaters’ sides.
The capitulary’s soap makers and the Italian soap craft are two early signs of soap as a workshop product.
The whale hunted by Ohthere and the carcass fought over in Iceland are the two earliest northern whale stories in this folio.
The Arabic oil words and the monks’ oil expertise are two routes by which Mediterranean oil culture survived into the north-west.
The cookbook’s dietetic chapters explain why its recipes use tail fat, olive oil and clarified butter as they do.
The bread and sweets recipes and the tail-fat frying come from the same Baghdad cookbook.
The Prophet’s oil and the monks’ lamp oil are two religions’ uses of the same Mediterranean substance.
A Tang monastery’s ever-burning lamp and a Chola temple’s perpetual lamp are the same offering fed by different fats.
Japan’s so and China’s ladder from milk to su show the Buddhist-age dairy world of East Asia.
Shea in the Sahel and sesame in south India are two tropical seed and nut fats pressed for local use in the same centuries.
The meat ban and the absence of herds are why Japanese cooking did without animal fat, in Ishige’s account.
Tang dairy fashion and the Buddhist ladder from milk to ghee belong to the same dairy moment.
Tang China’s dairy peak and Japan’s milk-skin tribute are the two Buddhist-age dairy worlds of East Asia.
Japan’s court kept a dairy tribute while its banquets did without oil.
The banquet dairy fats of Chang and the peak of Tang dairy consumption are the same observation from two historians.
Ti-hu is the summit of the Buddhist ladder from milk and of the pharmacopoeias that Needham cites.
Fried sesame cakes and the Tang calendar’s fourth-month seed pressing are the street and farm ends of the same oil trade.
The Frankish stewards’ accounts of bacon and fat and the autumn mast feeding of the estates’ pigs are two ends of the same pork economy.
Iran’s sesame crop and Baghdad’s sesame-oil bread are the same region’s sesame in the same century.
Birnirk’s Bering Strait hunters and Ohthere’s White Sea whaling are two marine-fat economies of the same centuries, at opposite ends of the Arctic.
Maya palm oil and Anglo-Saxon butter are two very different answers to the same universal need for dietary fat, one tropical and plant-based, one northern and animal-based.
Pemba’s uncertain sesame seed and Copán’s cultivated coyol palm are two very different, very differently evidenced fat stories of roughly the same centuries.
